claims.text: The relevant AlCrFeNiSi feedstock has a typical powder-size distribution of 15–53 μm.
Resonant acoustic mixing can coat AlCrFeNiSi powder uniformly with nanoscale Y2O3.
The proposed processing window uses inert-atmosphere L-PBF, millimeter-scale parts, and lower layer energy input than conventional high-thermal-load processing.
Y2O3 nanoparticles applied to the feedstock will remain dispersed throughout the printed AlCrFeNiSi component.
Dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles will act as heterogeneous nucleation sites during AlCrFeNiSi solidification.
Dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles will act as dispersion-strengthening agents in printed AlCrFeNiSi.
The Y2O3 dispersoids will modify solidification dynamics and grain structure.
The dispersoids will refine grains and interrupt the formation of large columnar grains.
Grain refinement caused by the dispersoids will reduce localized thermal gradients.
The dispersoid-mediated microstructure will reduce residual thermal stress.
Y2O3 dispersoids will inhibit defect formation during L-PBF.
Dispersion strengthening will increase the mechanical strength of printed AlCrFeNiSi.
Coated-powder components will have lower residual stress than components made under conventional high-thermal-load conditions.
Coated-powder components will have a finer and more homogeneous microstructure than the baseline components.
Coated-powder components will have higher tensile strength than the baseline components.
Coated-powder components will have greater ductility than the baseline components.
The benefits will be most pronounced for millimeter-scale components made from 15–53 μm powder and may not transfer to larger builds or substantially different powder morphologies.
The magnitude of the benefits will depend on dispersoid concentration, coating uniformity, and laser-processing parameters.

contradictions.description: The coating is presented as the single intervention, but the treatment condition also reduces energy input relative to the high-thermal-load baseline. Thus, the predicted comparison changes both powder functionalization and thermal input, confounding attribution to the coating.

The predicted outcome is relative to conventional high-thermal-load processing, whereas the falsification experiment compares coated and uncoated powders under identical parameters optimized for miniature fabrication. It therefore does not directly test the stated high-thermal-load comparator.
